author: Alyssa Tolman Wyoming Tribune Eagle
title: Cheyenne City Council narrows sixth-penny ballot to 11 projects totaling $74.25M | Local News | wyomingnews.com
text:
CHEYENNE – Members of the Cheyenne City Council have selected 11 projects to appear on the 2026 sixth-penny sales tax ballot, which will go before voters in the Aug. 18 primary election.
The list, which was presented and recommended by Mayor Patrick Collins, was discussed at the council’s Committee of the Whole meeting Wednesday evening.
Collection of money authorized during the last specific-purpose tax vote — which took place in November 2021 — is anticipated to be completed in the first quarter of 2026. If that happens as expected, sales tax would revert to 5% in Laramie County until the new projects are approved.
City Council members are required to submit the final ballot selections to the Laramie County Board of Commissioners for approval by April 6, and the commissioners must approve the list by May 5. Following approval, election notices will be published, and early voting will begin July 21.
For all of the initially proposed projects, the total estimated cost was $122 million. However, the city’s share of the ballot is only $74,250,000.
Here are the final projects that council members approved to appear on the ballot.
Fire Station #2 replacement
Cheyenne Fire Rescue’s (CFR) request for $12 million to help replace Station 2 on Fox Farm Road was approved to appear on the ballot.
The station was built in 1985, and the new one would be built on city-owned property at 503 W. College Drive to better align with city growth.
Fire apparatus replacement project
CFR is requesting $5,023,364 for apparatus replacement.
The money would cover replacement of three aging fire apparatus with two multi-purpose response vehicles, and one new 107-foot heavy-duty aerial ladder truck, replacing units originally placed in service in 1998, 2001 and 2008.
Fire equipment and communications replacement
The third and final request from CFR that was approved to appear on the ballot is $1,052,120 to replace dated personal protective gear, self-contained breathing apparatus, and purchase new radio systems and an attack hose.
CFR’s original request in this category was $1.8 million.
City street maintenance project
The city’s Engineering Department requested $9 million to be put on the ballot for proactive street maintenance. The money would be put toward crack sealing, patching, surface treatments and mill and overlay projects.
The Engineering Department receives $5 million annually from the fifth-penny sales tax for roads, which City Engineer Tom Cobb has previously told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle is not sufficient.
Initially, the department requested $15 million, but because the capacity for road construction contractors is low in Cheyenne, the amount was cut down.
Collins told council members Wednesday that because of the low capacity for contractors, the Engineering Department is only able to spend around $10 million on road maintenance per year.
“What we've learned is (contractors) are saturated,” Collins said. “There’s so much work to do, there’s less crews to do. … So the request that we’ve made is in recognition of that.”
CPD digital equipment and technology
Officials with the Cheyenne Police Department (CPD) originally requested $6,175,000 for four different projects, but the council only approved two projects – the first of which is $3.7 million for digital equipment and technology.
The money would be used to update and replace in-car cameras, body cameras and electronic control devices, along with associated digital evidence storage and investigative software.
CPD firearms training facility enhancement
The second CPD project the council approved is $1 million for the construction of an enclosed firearms training facility with modular interior walls for simunitions-based training, as well as resurfacing the existing pistol range deck with asphalt to improve safety and usability.
Greenway maintenance
Community Recreation and Events (CRE) asked for $3 million on the ballot to fund Greater Cheyenne Greenway repairs, upgrades and maintenance, as well as to help fund three new full-time Greenway staff positions.
There is currently 48 miles of Greenway in Cheyenne. Officials say the proposed improvements would enhance safety, accessibility and user experience.
The department also plans to perform foundation and wall repairs, lighting replacement, pavement repair and resurfacing, bridge maintenance and mowing.
The entire requested amount of $3 million was approved.
Greenway new construction and rehabilitation
Along with existing Greenway maintenance, the city’s Planning and Development Department is requesting $3 million to be combined with other funding sources for new Greenway construction and major rehabilitation projects.
The original request was $3.5 million.
Key projects under this section include rehabilitation of the Yellowstone Road underpass, Parsley Boulevard Greenway extension and completing the connection along Cribbon Avenue.
“The Greenway is one of those projects that, when it’s on the ballot, it touches every neighborhood of the city,” said Jim Walter, chair of the Greenway Advisory Council, at the meeting. “The Greenway, it’s in Ward 1, it’s in Ward 2, it’s in Ward 3. … It is one of the greatest amenities we have on the south side.”
Downtown improvements
Council members approved $4 million to go toward various improvements in the downtown area, which is $1 million below the City Council’s initial request.
Specific projects to be funded with this money include replacing two elevators in the Spiker Parking Garage, further renovations of the Cheyenne Depot Museum, construction of enclosed storage areas for trash and recycling containers, and curb and sidewalk improvements.
Municipal Building remodel
The city’s Department of Public Works originally requested $27 million to fund the renovation and modernization of the Cheyenne Municipal Building, but council members approved $22 million to go on the ballot.
The Municipal Building was built in the late 1970s, and officials say the HVAC system, plumbing and electrical systems are well beyond their life expectancy.
The project includes improvements to public service areas, office space reconfiguration, Americans with Disabilities Act accessibility upgrades, and associated furniture and equipment.
Vicki Nemecek, Public Works director, told council members Wednesday that the HVAC, plumbing and electrical have never been updated.
Nemecek also said the restrooms in the building are outdated and difficult to clean.
“We’ve painted, and we’ve done the best that we can,” Nemecek said. “We’ve put new carpet in. It’s lipstick on a pig. We’ve got a pig, and we’ve been putting lipstick on it for five decades. And we’re two decades past a major renovation.”
Johnson Pool replacement
CRE requested $10,474,516 to aid in the construction of a new pool that would replace the now-closed Johnson Pool, which was over 70 years old at the time of closing in August.
The new pool, which will have garage doors to allow both indoor and outdoor use, is intended to be larger and include more amenities. Project planning is approximately 65% complete.
Cut projects
Collins told council members about the remaining projects that did not make his list of recommendations.
These include replacing CFR’s Fire Station #6 for $9.77 million; renovating the Historic Pumphouse for $4 million; continuing the Reed Avenue Corridor project for $14.9 million; funding the city’s portion of the airline minimum revenue guarantee for $2.5 million; building an arts and aviation center in the historic airport terminal for $3.9 million; and funding CPD’s multi-purpose rescue and response vehicles, and a multi-bay storage building for $975,000 and $500,000, respectively.
The Reed Avenue Corridor project was approved on the last sixth-penny ballot in 2021 in the amount of $4 million, but council members later learned that amount would not be sufficient.
However, Collins told council members Wednesday that he’d rather leave it off the 2026 ballot because of ongoing issues regarding a railroad agreement with the Burlington Northern Railroad.
“We’ve been told it will take at least 18 months to get there,” Collins said. “I believe it would be irresponsible to put funding on a ballot when we don’t own the property, and we don’t have permission to construct.”
The council's vote
After more than two hours of discussion, council members approved the 11 ballot propositions, with Council Mark Rinne being the only “no” vote. The total amount approved adds up to exactly $74,250,000.
The City Council will approve the final ballot at its regularly scheduled meeting Jan. 26.
